deep.reconstruction:
The page has no derivations. It is one sheet (red crayon sheet number 9) of a large table of quadratic residues. It continues the previous sheet (columns 2 to 89, red 8) and leads into the next (columns 227 to 359, red 10).

Layout: the rows are the prime moduli p = 191, 193, 197, ..., 433, the same row set on all three sheets. The columns are the primes q = 97, 101, 103, ..., 223. A small circle in cell (p, q) means that q is a quadratic residue mod p, i.e. the Legendre symbol (q/p) = +1. An empty cell means (q/p) = -1. The diagonal cell q = p (row 191 and 193 territory near columns 191 and 193) is necessarily special.

Orientation was tested in a case where it matters, with p ≡ q ≡ 3 (mod 4), where (q/p) = -(p/q):
- (103/191) = +1 but (191/103) = -1. The cell (191, 103) carries a circle.
- (107/191) = +1 but (191/107) = -1. The cell (191, 107) carries a circle.
So the convention is 'column prime is a residue of the row modulus'. This is the same layout as Tabula II of the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (§99 ff.), which lists, for prime moduli, which of the small primes are residues.

The page thus extends that table from residue-primes up to 97 (as in the Disquisitiones) to residue-primes up to 223 and beyond (next sheet), for moduli 191 to 433.

How the entries were presumably found (my reconstruction, not written on the page): by quadratic reciprocity. For example:
- (97/191) = (191/97) = (94/97) = (2/97)(47/97) = (3/47) = -(47/3) = +1, so a circle.
- (101/191) = (90/101) = (2/101)(5/101)(9/101) = -1, so empty.
- (113/191) = (78/113) = (2/113)(3/113)(13/113) = 1·(-1)·1 = -1, so empty.
Other spot checks agree with the drawn circles: (97/197) = +1, (101/197) = +1, (103/199) = +1.

The pen strokes joining circles connect marked cells that are adjacent, horizontally (consecutive column primes) or vertically (consecutive row primes). The result is clusters ('polyominoes') of residues. These seem to be a visual or pattern-finding device, or an aid to checking and copying. They carry no additional arithmetic content that I can verify.

Other marks:
- The circled (5) is the archival folio number.
- 'Math. 1' and a number at the top right are later archival pencil marks.
errors: No arithmetic errors were found in the spot checks: (97/191)=+1, (101/191)=-1, (103/191)=+1, (107/191)=+1, (113/191)=-1, (97/197)=+1, (101/197)=+1, (103/199)=+1, all matching the circles. A full cell-by-cell verification against the image was not performed. Exact column alignment near the right-hand block (columns 179 to 223) is hard to read, so I make no claim about individual cells there.

results.what: Table of quadratic residue characters (q/p) for prime moduli p from 191 to 433 and primes q from 97 to 223, with adjacent residues graphically linked
results.modern_name: Table of Legendre symbols / quadratic residue table (extension of Disquisitiones Arithmeticae Tabula II)
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Disquisitiones Arithmeticae, 1801, Tabula II); later extensive tables by Jacobi (Canon arithmeticus, 1839) and others

results.what: Joining adjacent residue cells by lines to form visual clusters
results.modern_name: Graphical display of residue patterns (no standard name)

deep.surprise_reason: Gauss's computation of extensive quadratic residue tables is well known (Disquisitiones Tabula II and Nachlass tables). This sheet is an extension of that work, with only a minor curiosity in the line-linking of adjacent residues.

transcription_corrections: Row label '223' is written over a correction ('22[3]' with overwriting), but it reads 223 as expected in the prime sequence.
Top marks: 'Math. 1' (pencil, archival) above columns 103 to 109. The top-right pencil number looks like '48[9?]5' (archival), not part of Gauss's table.
Red crayon '9' is the sheet number in the sequence 8 (previous), 9, 10 (next). The circled '5' is the folio number.
Body: circles mean column prime q is a quadratic residue mod row prime p. Lines join only horizontally or vertically adjacent circles.
